summary:
Nobody knows who wrote Hebrews. Guesses have included Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, and Priscilla, and the third-century scholar Origen concluded that only God knows. It is not quite a letter either: it calls itself a "word of exhortation" (13:22) and reads like a sermon, the most sustained theological argument in the New Testament. The audience appears to be Jewish believers, worn down by pressure, who were tempted to drift back to the familiar world of synagogue and temple. The author's strategy is to argue that everything in that world pointed forward to Christ, so going back would mean trading the reality for the shadow.

The opening sets the terms: "On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son" (1:1-2). The argument then works through the audience's most revered figures and institutions, showing Jesus greater than each: the angels, Moses, Joshua, and finally the priesthood itself. The most intricate stretch argues from Melchizedek, the priest-king who appears briefly in Genesis 14 and Psalm 110, that Jesus holds a priesthood older than Levi's, and that his single sacrifice ends the system of repeated ones. Threaded between these arguments are urgent warnings against drifting away, whose implications interpreters still debate.

The payoff is practical. Because the high priest can sympathize, "let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence" (4:16). Chapter 11 rolls through Israel's history of faith, defined as "the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see" (11:1), and is honest that many died without receiving what was promised. Chapter 12 draws the conclusion: run with endurance, and "fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith" (12:2). The argument is dense; read it patiently, and let the warnings and encouragements land together.
